publication: Alexander of Aphrodisias On Fate (Duckworth, London; text, translation and commentary)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander HAS a libertarian (vs soft-determinist) conception of responsibility — but the label is used as a deliberate, hedged historiographical category, not asserted as Alexander's own self-description.
position_summary: Sharples distinguishes soft determinism (Chrysippus), hard determinism, and libertarianism (incompatibilist + indeterminist). The Greek 'to eph' hēmin' was shared by soft-determinists and libertarians, so its mere occurrence is not a safe guide; but Sharples holds it 'can be shown' that some thinkers, Alexander among them, have a libertarian rather than soft-determinist conception of responsibility, and only in such cases does he use 'freedom'. He is careful that the debate is conducted in terms of responsibility (to eph' hēmin), not freedom/free will, the latter term appearing only in Latin writers.
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato, esp. the eph' hēmin accounts (Fat. 181.5; 180.26-8; 199.9; 211.32 Bruns) — KG passage_alex_fat_15 / passage_alex_fat_38; cf. Cicero De Fato on 'soft determinism' of Chrysippus (cic_fat 41-43)
attested_quote: The Greek to eph' hēmin, 'what depends on us', like the English 'responsibility', was used both by libertarians and by soft determinists, though they differed as to what it involved; ... nevertheless it can be shown that some thinkers, Alexander among them, have a libertarian rather than a soft-determinist conception of responsibility, and in such cases I have not hesitated to use expressions like 'freedom'.

publication: Alexander of Aphrodisias On Fate (Duckworth, London)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander STIPULATES libertarian freedom but does not adequately ESTABLISH it: his libertarian conception of responsibility is genuine and unqualified (power for opposite courses of action, unrestricted), yet he fails to reconcile it with the rational element in human behaviour.
position_summary: Sharples reads Alexander's repeated descriptions of responsibility as power/capacity for opposite courses of action 'in terms of an unqualified, unrestricted possibility' — i.e. a robustly libertarian (two-sided, non-predetermined) requirement, objecting even to determination by a combination of internal AND external factors. But this is the careful hedge: Alexander 'faces very real difficulties in combining his libertarian position with an account of the rational element in human behaviour, and does not really solve it' — most acute in Mantissa XXII, where responsibility ends up identified with human weakness (a 'bizarre consequence'). So Alexander posits/requires libertarian freedom without giving it a coherent rational grounding.
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato (power for opposites: Fat. 180.5f., 180.20f., 180.26f., 181.5f., 181.3, 190.25, 199.9, 206.19, 211.32 Bruns; KG passage_alex_fat_12/13/15/28/36/38) and Mantissa XXII (170-172 Bruns)
attested_quote: He objects not just to determination of our actions by external causes alone, but to that resulting from a combination of internal and external factors; ... This shows that his repeated descriptions of responsibility in terms of the power or capacity for opposite courses of action are to be understood in terms of an unqualified, unrestricted possibility. ... he faces very real difficulties in combining his libertarian position with an account of the rational element in human behaviour, and does not really solve it. This problem is perhaps most acute ... in mantissa XXII, with bizarre consequences — responsibility being identified with human weakness.

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem (Phronesis 43.2)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander provides the EARLIEST UNAMBIGUOUS EVIDENCE for awareness of a 'free-will problem' — but the problem arose inadvertently, between systems, not as a position Alexander himself held within a free-will framework.
position_summary: Bobzien restricts 'free-will problem' to the modern compatibility problem (universal causal determinism of the 'same causes, same effects' type vs. indeterminist freedom). The earliest unambiguous evidence for awareness of any such problem occurs in Alexander: it resembles modern problems in combining a 'same causes, same effects' determinism (Fat. 192.22) with a concept of indeterminist freedom — but WITHOUT invoking a concept of the will. The problem is a 'stalemate' between the Stoic compatibilist-determinist position and Alexander's Peripatetic 'seemingly libertarian' one; it emerged inadvertently from the confrontation of refined Stoic determinism with a two-sided, potestative eph' hēmin read into Aristotle.
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato 192.22-4 ('same circumstances → same effect' principle, KG passage_alex_fat_22); eph' hēmin as power of choosing opposites, Fat. 181.5 (passage_alex_fat_15) and Fat. 180.26-8 (passage_alex_fat_15)
attested_quote: The earliest unambiguous evidence for the awareness of any kind of 'free-will problem' occurs in Alexander of Aphrodisias. It resembles the problems modern philosophers discuss in that it is concerned with a theory of universal causal determinism which contains a principle of the type 'same causes, same effects,' and in that it involves a concept of indeterminist freedom without invoking a concept of the will.

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem (Phronesis 43.2)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander STOPS SHORT of a concept of free will: he assembled all the ingredients of acting-from-free-will, but they do not add up, chiefly because he holds the soul to be corporeal.
position_summary: This is Bobzien's decisive qualification against calling Alexander a libertarian/inventor of free will. She concedes Alexander 'has collected all the ingredients required for a notion of acting from free-will' — a two-sided power (exousia) of decision that is not necessitated by external or internal factors, is exercised through deliberation, and is separable from the agent's character and even reason, yielding the possibility that the same agent in the same circumstances chooses differently. Yet 'all these points do not add up to choosing and acting from free-will,' because for Alexander the soul is not separable from the body and is in principle susceptible to causal impacts, leaving no suitable place for an independent decision-making faculty. Hence 'Alexander stops short of a concept of free will.'
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato — two-sided exousia of decision (Fat. 180.26-8, 181.5, KG passage_alex_fat_15) and corporeality of the soul; Mantissa XXII/XXIII (174.35-9)
attested_quote: This is so despite the fact that he has collected all the ingredients required for a notion of acting from free-will: he has endowed human beings with a two-sided power (exousia) of decision making ... But all these points do not add up to 'choosing and acting from free-will,' since for Alexander the human soul is not separable from the body and in principle susceptible to causal impacts. ... Alexander stops short of a concept of free will, due it seems in part to the fact that he believes the human soul to be corporeal.

publication: The Inadvertent Conception and Late Birth of the Free-Will Problem (Phronesis 43.2)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander's contribution is a conceptual SHIFT (capability → exousia/authority over opposites), introducing a decision-making faculty — a step toward 'free decision' — but he himself has no free-will problem within his own system (he secures freedom by simply denying pre-determination).
position_summary: Bobzien identifies Alexander's specific innovation in the genealogy: the replacement, in the account of eph' hēmin, of 'being capable of' (dynasthai) by 'having the power or authority (exousia) over,' which 'introduces a decision making faculty, and thus leads to a concept of free decision' — probably a fusion of Epictetan and Aristotelian elements; plus the addition of choice (hairesis) to action. But Alexander himself 'had no free-will problem,' because, not believing in universal divine providence, he secures freedom to do otherwise by simply denying pre-determination of human actions. The genuine free-will problem becomes pressing only later, in Platonist and Christian philosophy (theological determinism), not in Alexander's physical-determinism context.
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato — eph' hēmin accounts (Fat. 181.5, 180.26-8; KG passage_alex_fat_15); shift dynasthai → exousia; cf. Epictetus' prohairesis
attested_quote: Second, the replacement in the account of 'being capable of' by 'having the power or authority (exousia) over' introduces a decision making faculty, and thus leads to a concept of free decision — the result probably of a fusion of Epictetan and Aristotelian elements.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (Sather Classical Lectures 68, ed. A.A. Long, D. Sedley)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander is the ANCESTOR of the (later) free-will notion of being able, in the very same circumstances, to choose between A and B — but for Frede this is a CONFUSED, incoherent dead-end, not the genuine notion of a free will (which Frede locates in the Stoics/Epictetus).
position_summary: Frede holds the genuine notion of a free will originated in later Stoicism (Epictetus); Alexander represents the rival Peripatetic line that gets it wrong. Alexander narrows eph' hēmin to assent based on rational scrutiny of impressions (taking over Carneades' unforced-assent notion of the voluntary) and makes freedom (eleutheron/autexousion) a condition of responsibility. But by insisting that, under identical internal AND external conditions, one can still choose and act otherwise (De Fato 192.22ff), he comes 'very close to Dihle's favored notion of a will which decides ... independently of the desires and beliefs of the person,' and is driven into 'a hopeless tangle.' Frede: 'it is in Alexander that we find the ancestor of the notion that to have a free will is to be able, in the very same circumstances, to choose between doing A and doing B. Unfortunately ... Alexander is not able to provide a coherent account of how such a free will is supposed to be possible.' Two reasons for the tangle: he misunderstood Stoic determinism (a choice can be free though it has a good explanation in antecedent causes), and he has a mistaken notion of merit/desert (as if merit lay in not choosing to act otherwise).
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato XIV (183.27ff, voluntary = unforced assent; KG passage_alex_fat_14), De Fato XXVIII (199.16ff, Stoic wise-man freedom; passage_alex_fat_28), De Fato XXXVIII (211.27ff, autexousion/eleutheron; passage_alex_fat_38), De Fato 192.22ff (same circumstances, choose otherwise; passage_alex_fat_22); Mantissa XXII; cf. Carneades (cic_fat 23, 31)
attested_quote: Here we have come very close to Dihle's favored notion of a will which decides or chooses in some mysterious way that is independent not only of the external objects of desire but also of the desires and beliefs of the person. ... it is in Alexander that we find the ancestor of the notion that to have a free will is to be able, in the very same circumstances, to choose between doing A and doing B. Unfortunately, though, but also as we would expect, Alexander is not able to provide a coherent account of how such a free will is supposed to be possible.

publication: A Free Will: Origins of the Notion in Ancient Thought (Sather Classical Lectures 68)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander's libertarian 'ability to do otherwise in the same circumstances' rests on TWO confusions and is therefore a philosophical error, not a genuine advance toward free will.
position_summary: Frede diagnoses why Alexander's position fails. First, 'he did not sufficiently understand Stoic determinism, so he did not see that a choice might be no less free for having a perfectly good explanation in terms of antecedent causes' — the wise person 'would have to be crazy not to make the choice he does ... but this does not make his choice unfree.' Second, 'Alexander has a mistaken notion of merit, as if merit were a matter of not choosing to act otherwise.' On Frede's view the merit of a virtuous action lies in the action and its motivation, not in the open possibility of having chosen something crazy; 'we deserve no credit for not being crazy ... and we have no reason for complaint, if we are not free to do crazy things.' This is the 'dead-end' verdict: Alexander's two-sided freedom is born of misreading the Stoics and of a juridical (desert-based) confusion peculiar to his age.
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato 192.22ff (choose otherwise in same circumstances; KG passage_alex_fat_22); the Mantissa XXII inference that ability-to-choose-otherwise is human weakness
attested_quote: Alexander got into this tangle mainly for two reasons. First, he did not sufficiently understand Stoic determinism, so he did not see that a choice might be no less free for having a perfectly good explanation in terms of antecedent causes. The wise person would have to be crazy not to make the choice he does, even though that choice is not impossible. But this does not make his choice unfree. Second, Alexander has a mistaken notion of merit, as if merit were a matter of not choosing to act otherwise. ... We deserve no credit for not being crazy or for not choosing to do crazy things, and we have no reason for complaint, if we are not free to do crazy things.

publication: Aristotle and Determinism (Peeters, Louvain; = collected essays, incl. 'Human Initiative: Limits and Constants')
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander is an EXCELLENT but TENDENTIOUS interpreter of Aristotle: in the polemical De Fato he is 'reticent' and distorts Aristotle's own position to widen the space of indeterminist freedom — so his apparent libertarianism is partly a polemical artefact, not a faithful reading of Aristotle.
position_summary: Donini contrasts Alexander's (correct) exegesis of Aristotle in the commentaries with his (skewed) handling in the De Fato. In his commentary on the Prior Analytics Alexander rightly distributes human actions between 'for the most part' events (regular effects of character/proairesis) and 'whichever-of-two-ways' (hopoter' etyche) events, faithfully combining NE III with De Interpretatione 9 — 'his Aristotelian interpretation is correct throughout.' Yet in De Fato chs. XI and XII, 'in quite unaristotelian fashion he emphasizes as much as possible the abundance of alternatives always available to the acting subject,' is 'careful not to associate the object of deliberation ... with a precise reference to frequencies of occurrence,' and never mentions 'for the most part' or ad utrumlibet events. Donini's verdict: this silence/distortion is motivated — 'for a philosopher engaged in a harsh polemic against determinism, this was a result worth some reticence and some distortion of Aristotle's thought,' since removing 'for the most part' as the object of choice 'could mean widening the scope of freedom of will and opening greater spaces of contingency to moral choice.'
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato XI (178.15ff Bruns; KG passage_alex_fat_11) and XII (180.12ff; passage_alex_fat_12) on deliberation/decision; Ethical Problems (Quaest. IV) 160.4-19 Br.; vs. Alexander In An. Pr. 162.31-163.7; Aristotle NE III 1112a21-b12 (esp. 1112b8-9) and De Int. 9
attested_quote: although — in quite unaristotelian fashion — he emphasizes as much as possible the abundance of alternatives always available to the acting subject, he is careful not to associate the object of deliberation, as Aristotle does in NE III or in de Interpretatione 9, with a precise reference to frequencies of occurrence: he never mentions 'for the most part' events, nor the rival group of ad utrumlibet events. ... removing 'for the most part' as the particular object of choice and deliberation ... could mean widening the scope of freedom of will and opening greater spaces of contingency to moral choice. For a philosopher engaged in a harsh polemic against determinism, this was a result worth some reticence and some distortion of Aristotle's thought.

publication: The Dramatization of Determinism: Alexander of Aphrodisias' De Fato (Phronesis 27.3)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander has NOT given the Stoics a fair trial: his case for indeterminist free will rests on 'dramatizing' determinism (treating regular causation as ironclad necessity) and on misreading Stoic causal theory — so his libertarianism is rhetorically inflated and philosophically not established against a reasonable Stoic compatibilism.
position_summary: D. Frede reconstructs a 'reasonable' Stoic position and argues Alexander's reductio method distorts both Stoa and Peripatos. Alexander limits fate to the efficient/moving cause (= nature, 169.18ff), excluding form and telos, in an un-Aristotelian shift driven by the need to answer the Stoa. His central move against Stoic compatibilism is the 'dramatization' of determinism: from invariance he infers invariability, from invariability 'dire/ironclad necessity,' and from 'if nothing interferes' he slides to 'if nothing CAN interfere' (he coins the adverb katēnankasmenōs, 'necessitatedly,' 185.15, 190.8, 191.12, 200.2, 206.6). D. Frede holds the Stoic 'necessitation' may be the harmless 'omne quod fit quando fit necesse est fieri,' so Alexander 'has not given them a fair trial when he brushes aside their attempt to preserve free will'; he 'does not review their causal theory properly' (192.18) and misunderstands the antecedent/principal-cause distinction. Net: Alexander defends to eph' hēmin / autexousios man, but his anti-determinist case is undercut by rhetorical dramatization rather than decisively established.
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato: fate = efficient cause (169.18ff; KG passage_alex_fat_6), katēnankasmenōs (185.15, 190.8, 191.12, 200.2, 206.6; passage_alex_fat_15/30/36), perfunctory summary of Stoic causes (192.18; passage_alex_fat_22), eph' hēmin / autexousios (181.14, 208.3; passage_alex_fat_15/38); Cicero De Fato 36, 41-44 (causae adiuvantes/principales; cic_fat 36, 41, 44)
attested_quote: The dramatization proceeds, in sum, as follows. From invariance one concludes that there is invariability, from invariability that there is 'dire', 'ironclad' necessity. And from the condition 'if nothing interferes' one proceeds to 'if nothing can interfere'. ... I just want to point out that he has not given them a fair trial when he brushes aside their attempt to preserve free will on the thesis of a careful causal distinction ... He does not review their causal theory properly as his perfunctory summary shows (192,18) when compared to other sources.

publication: Alexander of Aphrodisias: A Source of Origen's Philosophy (Philosophie antique 14)
debate: Is Alexander of Aphrodisias a libertarian / De Fato reception
stance: Alexander is a ROBUST anti-determinist and a positive SOURCE/ANCESTOR — Origen very probably knew Alexander's works (read in Plotinus' school) and both refuted Stoic determinism with very similar arguments; treats Alexander's defense of to eph' hēmin / autexousion as a substantive, transmissible doctrine of freedom rather than a confused dead-end.
position_summary: Against the deflationary readings (Bobzien's 'stops short', M. Frede's 'incoherent ancestor'), Ramelli emphasizes continuity and influence: it is 'very probable that Origen knew Alexander of Aphrodisias' works, which were read at the school of Plotinus, and drew inspiration from them,' with Origen's Peri Archōn probably inspired in structure by Alexander's homonymous work, and the formula ēn pote hote ouk ēn first used by Alexander and Origen. On free will specifically (per the KG node grounded in this work), both Alexander and Origen refuted Stoic determinism with very similar arguments — praise/blame and the efficacy of petitionary prayer — and Alexander 'deemed Stoic compatibilism between Fate and free will untenable and dangerous for moral life because it excluded responsibility and ruled out to eph' hēmin.' Ramelli thus positions Alexander as a constructive ancestor of the Christian autexousion tradition.
contested_locus: Alexander De Fato (anti-determinist arguments from praise/blame and prayer; eph' hēmin / autexousion) and Peri Archōn; cf. Origen, Peri Archōn III.1 (De Princ. on autexousion); formula ēn pote hote ouk ēn
attested_quote: It is very probable that Origen knew Alexander of Aphrodisias' works, which were read at the school of Plotinus, and drew inspiration from them. ... The expression ἦν ποτε ὅτε οὐκ ἦν, very interestingly, was used for the first time exactly by Alexander and Origen.
